N5 MAX results

Minisforum N5 MAX · Ryzen AI Max+ 395 · 128 GB unified memory · 5× 4 TB NVMe

What the N5 MAX is good for, and how to set it up.

Measured results from a seven-stage campaign, organised by the workloads we bought the box for. Four of the five NVMe slots run at PCIe Gen4 ×1 and one at ×4, so the layout you choose matters more than the SSD.

Final campaign data · 2026-10-08 Editorial seal pending Publisher review Labels: PROVISIONAL = ≥2× spread vs its own history · non-steady = failed the steadiness rail

Use case 1

Local AI and RAG box

You want to run local LLMs, embeddings and a RAG index on the same box that stores the documents.

Recommended

ZFS RAIDZ1 across all five NVMe · models resident in memory · HIP for prefill and embeddings, Vulkan for chat

  • 14.11 TiB usable and 7.83 GB/s cold sequential reads for model files and documents.
  • Keeps 93.51 % of its read speed with a drive out, so the index stays usable during a failure.
  • Once a model is loaded, the pool makes no difference to inference speed (table below), so choose the pool for storage reasons.

What this means

  • MoE models are the sweet spot. gpt-oss-120b decodes at 53.12 tok/s (HIP) and 57.25 tok/s (Vulkan). The dense 27B model manages 12.59 tok/s.
  • Pick the backend per job. Vulkan decodes faster on all four models run on both backends. HIP prefills faster and loads much faster: gpt-oss-120b cold-loads in 11.256 s on HIP against 49.375 s on Vulkan.
  • Long context costs decode speed. At 55k tokens gpt-oss-120b keeps 59 % of its empty-context decode speed.

Our figures here come from separate runs using the vendor's llama-bench invocation, so they differ slightly from the table above. Vendor figures are quoted from Minisforum's product page, which states no test conditions beyond all layers offloaded and flash attention on.

What the data does not support

  • Vector-database or embedding-index IO patterns were not benchmarked. A small-recordsize dataset or zvol for the vector DB follows from the random-IO results, not from a direct test.
  • KV-cache quantisation, prefill-under-decode scheduling and image or video generation have no published results.

Use case 2

AI + VM server (Proxmox)

You want VMs and containers with databases alongside the AI workloads.

Recommended

ZFS RAID10 on the four Gen4 ×1 drives for VM disks (zvols) · keep sync enabled

  • Sync 16K writes, which databases and VM guests depend on, run at 1,675 IOPS on RAID10 against 415 IOPS on RAIDZ1.
  • Mixed 70/30 IO reaches 104,485 IOPS. The cost is capacity: 6.71 TiB usable.
  • If capacity matters more than sync speed, one RAIDZ1 pool with VM zvols also works (14.11 TiB).
LayoutTiBSync 16KRand write 4KRand write 16KMixed 70/30
ZFS RAID10 · 4× ×16.711,67540,74051,195104,485
ZFS RAID10 + hot spare6.711,63125,04838,95683,997
ZFS RAIDZ1 · 5-wide14.1141518,86530,495757 PROVISIONAL
ZFS RAIDZ2 · 5-wide10.2142810,35710,91227,755

What this means

  • The ×1 slots don't slow small-block IO much. One drive at ×4 does sync writes 1.09 × as fast as at ×1, against 3.27 × for sequential reads. VM responsiveness is drive-bound, not lane-bound.
  • ARC metadata caching helps reads, not sync. With primarycache=metadata, 4K random reads on RAID10 rise to 183,883 IOPS, but RAIDZ1 sync writes fall to 256 IOPS.
  • No power-loss protection. The NM790 has none, so never set sync=disabled on VM storage.

What the data does not support

  • A SLOG device on the ×4 slot was not tested, so there is no figure for RAIDZ1 + SLOG.
  • The five 3.5″ SATA bays (shared Gen3 ×2 uplink) were not benchmarked. Using them as a backup pool is reasonable, but there is no data for it.
  • Random IO can't be ranked across ZFS, btrfs and mdadm: ZFS ran on zvols and the others on files.
  • Putting the OS on the ×4 drive alongside a RAID10 array is the intended layout, but the OS placement itself was not benchmarked.

Use case 3

Media and file archive

You want bulk storage for media, backups and shared files that survives drive failures.

Recommended

ZFS RAIDZ2 5-wide for two-failure tolerance · ZFS RAIDZ1 if you need the extra capacity · scrub monthly

  • RAIDZ2: 10.21 TiB, 8.911 GB/s cold reads, and 59.55 % of read speed with a drive out.
  • RAIDZ1: 14.11 TiB and 93.51 % degraded, rebuilt in 29 min.
LayoutTiBSeq read GB/sSeq write GB/sDegraded readRebuildWrite amp
ZFS RAIDZ114.117.830.71893.51 %1,740 s1.245 ×
ZFS RAIDZ210.218.9110.96159.55 %1,690 s1.679 ×
btrfs raid514.439.0344.0665.87 %3,720 s1.255 ×
btrfs raid610.719.0262.725.86 %6,380 s1.764 ×

Don't compare the seq-write column across ZFS and btrfs: the ZFS cells fully preconditioned the drives first and the btrfs cells did not. Under the same stage-7 protocol, after the same 50 % fill, RAIDZ1 wrote 4.499 GB/s and btrfs raid5 2.78 GB/s.

What this means

  • ZFS keeps serving when a drive dies; btrfs parity doesn't. btrfs raid5 drops to 5.87 % of its read speed with a drive out and takes 62 min to rebuild.
  • Healthy reads are faster than 10GbE on every candidate. A single client will be network-bound on reads. Network throughput itself was not measured.
  • Big sustained writes slow down on these drives. In a no-failure control the same write sequence returned 66.58 % and 67.71 % of its first sequential-write speed: the NM790 slows once its cache is spent. Plan large ingests with that in mind.
  • Thermals are fine. A one-hour mixed soak on RAIDZ1 held 0.886 GB/s steady with drives peaking at 59.85 °C.
  • USB ingest. Copying from a USB-attached NVMe into RAIDZ1 ran at 905.6 MB/s and back out at 376.2 MB/s. Post-campaign run on a different OS image; the enclosure fell back from UAS, so treat it as a floor.

What the data does not support

  • SMB/NFS throughput over the 2×10GbE ports and the SATA bay tier were not measured.
  • The btrfs raid5/6 write-hole (unclean shutdown) test was built but not run.

Use case 4

Models larger than memory

You want to run frontier-size models by streaming weights from the NVMe pool.

No recommendation

The data does not support streaming models for interactive use on this box.

  • Decode stays between 1.09 tok/s and 1.78 tok/s on every pool tested.
  • Load time is where pools differ: Kimi K2 loads in 38.334 s from btrfs and 181.147 s from ZFS with primarycache=all.

What the data does not support

  • Streaming from a ZFS dataset with primarycache=metadata was not tested, so we can't say whether it closes the ZFS load gap.

Layouts to avoid, and why

btrfs raid5/6 for primary data

Fastest when healthy (9.034 GB/s), but degraded reads fall to 5.87 % and raid6 takes 106 min to rebuild. The upstream data write hole is unmitigated (-m raid1c3 protects metadata only) and was not tested here.

mdadm raid5/6 for VMs or databases

Fastest sequential writes (5.04 GB/s), but 16K random writes collapse to 2,489 IOPS (raid5) and 2,313 IOPS (raid6). Fine for bulk sequential work only.

btrfs raid10 for single-stream reads

Reads only 3.616 GB/s cold, against 7.223 GB/s for mdadm raid10 on the same drives. The cause is not established.

The platform in one paragraph

Each of the four ×1 slots carries one drive at about 1.8 GB/s; the ×4 slot reads 5.888 GB/s. Striping across all five lifts sequential reads to 9.034 GB/s (btrfs raid5) and 9.035 GB/s (mdadm raid5), the fastest pools measured. Warm reads hit the memory ceiling (about 36.272 GB/s on every layout) and say nothing about the array.

Method, briefly

  • Hardware: five Lexar NM790 4 TB (DRAM-less, no power-loss protection), labelled SN1–SN5. SN1–SN4 on Gen4 ×1, SN5 on Gen4 ×4.
  • Storage figures are fio Protocol B published cases: one sealed case per test, with a steadiness check. Non-steady and PROVISIONAL values are labelled and never used for a recommendation.
  • Cold means primarycache=none on ZFS or dropped caches on btrfs/mdadm. Runs with a link-downtrained drive were excluded.
  • AI figures are llama.cpp llama-bench (HIP/ROCm and Vulkan/RADV), f16 KV cache.
  • Every number on this page is read from data/sealed-metrics.json; hover a figure to see its source key.
